tagline: An old toll-road corridor through a landscape of water supply
intro: Route 58 follows Black Rock Turnpike north through Easton, passing Hemlock and Aspetuck reservoirs, which supply much of Greater Bridgeport’s drinking water. A 3.1-mile section near Hemlock Reservoir is a designated scenic highway. The surrounding town developed slowly among rough hills along the Aspetuck River.

The turnpike name joins two separate road ventures. In 1797, the Fairfield, Weston, and Redding Turnpike was chartered to improve the route north from Easton village through Redding Ridge into Bethel. In 1832, the road from Black Rock harbor to Easton village became a public toll road. The modern Route 58 number dates to the 1932 state highway renumbering.

Travel north from Fairfield into Easton along Black Rock Turnpike, also called Black Rock Road within Easton. Hemlock Reservoir comes before Aspetuck Reservoir on this northbound journey. Farther along Black Rock Turnpike, the Bradley-Hubbell House overlooks Aspetuck Reservoir, a reminder that the water-supply landscape includes former farmland.

moments.title: Hemlock Reservoir
moments.text: Hemlock Reservoir’s dam was completed in 1914; the reservoir supplies water to Fairfield, Bridgeport and nearby towns. Its connections extend beyond the water beside the road: an underground aqueduct carries diverted water from Saugatuck Reservoir to Aspetuck Reservoir. Water is also diverted from Aspetuck into Hemlock, which then flows into the Mill River.

moments.title: Redding Road
moments.text: On April 25, 1777, British troops under General William Tryon marched toward Danbury to destroy homes, warehouses and ammunition stores. They used Redding Road, which paralleled present Route 58 south of Easton center and followed its alignment north of the center. The northern road became a chartered turnpike twenty years later, carrying the names Fairfield, Weston and Redding.

moments.title: Bradley-Hubbell House
moments.text: The Bradley-Hubbell House overlooks a reservoir that swallowed much of its farmland. Built in 1816 for Aljah and Elizabeth Bradley, the house has a traditional central chimney and Federal-style details, including oval windows in the gables. The family sold the property to Bridgeport Hydraulic Company in 1912; the company leased the house to its employee Franklin Hubbell. The house was donated to the Easton Historical Society in 1998. At 535 Black Rock Turnpike, its view is over Aspetuck Reservoir. John Dimon Bradley, the couple’s son, left a memoir describing life on what was mainly a subsistence farm.
